title: The Distant Weather
premise: Wren Delacroix, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, returns to their late grandmother's condemned house to sort her belongings before demolition. Behind a wardrobe they find a box of letters she wrote but never sent—letters that reveal she witnessed a drowning decades ago and stayed silent, letting an innocent man carry the blame. As Wren translates the letters back into the fading mother tongue, they must decide whether to expose the truth, knowing it will implicate the grandmother they loved and upend a family built on the silence. In the end, Wren delivers the letters to the wronged man's surviving daughter on the demolition date itself, choosing justice over inheritance and speaking the last fluent sentences of the dying language aloud.
about_author: Coral Yarrow grew up between two languages in a coastal town that no longer appears on most maps. Her fiction explores what families bury and what weather eventually uncovers.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Calendar
chapters.summary: Wren, in close third person, translates a contract in the city and realizes they can no longer recall the word for 'threshold' in their grandmother's tongue. A letter arrives: the house will be demolished in six weeks. The emotional beat is quiet dread—the sense of living on borrowed ground.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Arriving at the house, Wren finds it half-gutted by salvagers. Moving the wardrobe to check for rot, they uncover a tin box of unsent letters, all addressed to a name Wren doesn't recognize: Edda Voss. POV stays with Wren; the beat is vertigo, the past suddenly physical.

chapters.title: A Language of Half-Words
chapters.summary: Wren begins reading the first letter but stumbles—the handwriting uses dialect words they've lost. Flashbacks to childhood summers with Grandmother Maren establish warmth now shadowed. Beat: tenderness curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Drowned Boy
chapters.summary: The 1974 letter describes a boy drowning at the quarry and names a man, Tomas Lindqvist, who 'took the weight.' Wren researches: Tomas served eight years for manslaughter. POV alternates with interpolated letter text. Beat: cold shock.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Remember
chapters.summary: Wren visits Halvard, an elderly neighbor, who speaks fondly of Maren but goes silent when Tomas's name surfaces. His wife pulls Wren aside: 'Ask your grandmother's letters, not us.' Beat: the town as accomplice.

chapters.title: Translation as Betrayal
chapters.summary: Working through more letters, Wren confronts the translator's dilemma—each rendering is a choice. They realize Maren wrote these letters as confession and never sent them. Beat: complicity; Wren recognizes their own talent for not-sending.

chapters.title: Edda Voss
chapters.summary: Wren locates records: Edda was Tomas's daughter, now living two towns over. A first drive-by of her house ends in retreat. Beat: fear of confrontation, the pull toward invisibility.

chapters.title: The Quarry in Winter
chapters.summary: Wren walks the quarry where the boy drowned, now fenced and scheduled for development. A memory surfaces—Maren once brought them here and wept without explanation. Beat: grief arriving ahead of understanding.

chapters.title: The Second Box
chapters.summary: Behind loose plaster, Wren finds photographs and a second, shorter correspondence: Maren writing to herself, rehearsing confession across thirty years. Beat: horror at the discipline of silence.

chapters.title: Cousins at the Table
chapters.summary: Family gathers to divide the estate. Cousin Britt wants the land sold fast; when Wren mentions papers found, Britt's face closes. Beat: the family as interested party; inheritance revealed as hush money.

chapters.title: What Britt Knows
chapters.summary: Britt admits Maren told her 'something about the quarry' years ago and made her promise never to ask again. She begs Wren to let the demolition bury it. Beat: temptation, the comfort of finished stories.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: Midpoint. Wren translates the final unsent letter, dated three months before Maren's death: 'I am ready to be found out.' The emotional beat turns from dread to obligation—if Maren was ready, someone must do the finding.

chapters.title: The Daughter's Door
chapters.summary: Wren knocks on Edda Voss's door and loses their nerve, leaving only a note. That night Edda calls: 'I know why you came. Come back with everything.' Beat: terror and relief braided together.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: At Edda's kitchen table, Wren reads the letters aloud, translating haltingly. Edda corrects words her father used, unknowingly restoring Wren's lost vocabulary. Beat: language returning through shared grief.

chapters.title: Halvard's Confession
chapters.summary: Confronted, Halvard admits he helped Maren move the body's discovery away from her property line and kept quiet ever since. He gives Wren one more document. Beat: the town's architecture of silence exposed.

chapters.title: The Document
chapters.summary: It's Maren's sworn statement, never filed, naming the true sequence of events—including that the boy's death involved another child present that night. Beat: escalation; the truth is larger than one woman's guilt.

chapters.title: Whose Name Was On It
chapters.summary: Wren deciphers that the other child was Britt's father—meaning the family fortune traces to the cover-up. Rising action peaks: exposing Maren exposes everyone. Beat: fury and vertigo.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Britt offers Wren money and a lawyer to stay quiet; Wren refuses. Family fractures permanently. Alone in the house, Wren speaks Maren's final letter aloud in the old language and understands it fully for the first time. Beat: resolve.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax. At a small public gathering arranged with Edda and a local archivist, Wren reads the letters and statement aloud, in both languages, before neighbors including Halvard and Britt. The town must hear its own history. Beat: exposure as release.

chapters.title: Aftermath, or Weather
chapters.summary: Consequences ripple: a historical inquiry opens, Britt cuts contact, Halvard dies within the month, seemingly lighter. Wren feels neither vindicated nor forgiven—just unburdened and unmoored. Beat: the cost of justice outside the law.

chapters.title: The Last Fluent Sentence
chapters.summary: On demolition day, Wren stands at the fence and speaks the closing lines of Maren's final letter in the dying language, then translates them once into English so they can travel further. Beat: elegy; giving the language away to save it.

chapters.title: Owner of Nothing, Keeper Of
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Wren declines the inheritance settlement and instead funds, with Edda, a small memorial stone at the quarry bearing the drowned boy's name. Translating a new book, Wren finds the missing words keep arriving. Final beat: tenancy becomes stewardship; memory, tended, outlasts buildings.
